summary: Redefines selected ICMP messages so they can carry more than the original information. An extension structure at the end of the message, with its own header and objects, holds extra data that applications may require. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4884 lets certain Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) errors carry structured extra information, such as details used by diagnostic tools. A length field tells software where the quoted original packet ends and the added information begins, while padding helps older software continue to parse messages.

subtitle: Adds a safe way for selected ICMP errors to carry structured extra information.

tldr.problem: Some ICMP error messages include part of the original packet but do not say how long that part is, so extra data cannot be reliably separated from it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a length field for the original datagram and defines an extension header followed by typed objects at the end of eligible ICMP messages.
tldr.outcome: Applications can read additional information while retaining the original error data. RFC 4884 updates RFC 792 and RFC 4443 and is later updated by RFC 8335.

today: RFC 4884 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 792 and RFC 4443. It is updated by RFC 8335.

sections.title: Why ICMP Needs a Length Field
sections.content:
Selected ICMPv4 and ICMPv6 errors quote the start of the packet that caused the error. The quoted portion can vary in length, but the original message formats did not identify its boundary.

Without that boundary, appending more data would leave applications unable to tell whether bytes belonged to the quoted packet or to an extension. RFC 4884 updates selected messages with a length attribute and defines a common extension structure.
sections.plainLanguage: An ICMP error can include part of the packet that caused it, but the quoted part has no stated length. RFC 4884 adds that length so a receiver can find any extra information that follows.

sections.title: Where Extensions Can Appear
sections.content:
The extension structure may be appended to ICMPv4 Destination Unreachable, Time Exceeded, and Parameter Problem messages, and to ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable and Time Exceeded messages. The RFC does not permit it on the other listed message types.

The original-datagram length uses 32-bit words in ICMPv4 and 64-bit words in ICMPv6. When extensions are present, the quoted datagram must include at least 128 octets and is zero-padded to the relevant boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: Only specified ICMP error messages can carry this extension. Their length field measures the quoted packet in fixed-size words, and padding aligns the end of that packet before the extension starts.

sections.title: The Extension Header and Objects
sections.content:
An ICMP extension structure contains one extension header followed by one or more objects. The header includes a version, reserved bits, and a checksum; an all-zero checksum means no checksum was transmitted.

Each object has a 16-bit length, an 8-bit class number, an 8-bit type within that class, and a payload. Applications may process objects they recognize and ignore others; an unknown object does not by itself make the ICMP message malformed.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension begins with a header and then carries one or more typed objects. Each object states its size and type, so software can skip information it does not recognize.

sections.title: Compatibility with Older Software
sections.content:
Older applications may treat extension bytes as if they were part of the original datagram. The RFC places extensions after at least 128 octets of quoted data and requires additional padding, reducing the chance that older parsers will mistake the extension for important packet fields.

Some older traceroute implementations recognize extensions at a fixed position but ignore the new length field. Newer implementations must treat a zero length as no extension; the RFC also requires a non-compliant mode so traceroute can handle older non-compliant replies during transition.
sections.plainLanguage: Older tools may not understand the new length field. The minimum quoted data and padding help them cope, while updated diagnostic tools have a separate mode for older replies.

sections.title: Validation and Security
sections.content:
Applications that receive ICMP extensions must check their syntax and verify the extension checksum. Incorrect length values or malformed structures can cause memory errors such as buffer overruns.

This RFC does not change when routers send ICMP messages and says it does not expose routers to new denial-of-service attacks. Routers may still need to limit the rate of ICMP messages they send.
sections.plainLanguage: Receivers must validate lengths and check the extension checksum before using the data. These checks help prevent malformed messages from causing software errors.
